content.page_title: Heart failure: epidemiology, aetiology, natural history and prognosis (excerpt)

aetiology.summary: The most common causes of heart failure vary by geography. In Western-type and developed countries, coronary artery disease (CAD) and hypertension are predominant factors.
aetiology.note_on_ischaemic_aetiology: HFmrEF resembles HFrEF with a higher frequency of underlying CAD compared with HFpEF.

natural_history_and_prognosis.overall: Prognosis of heart failure has improved since the first treatment trials but remains poor; improvement has been largely confined to patients with HFrEF.
natural_history_and_prognosis.mortality_observational_vs_trials: Mortality rates are higher in observational studies than in clinical trials.

cohort_findings.study: Combined Framingham Heart Study and CHS cohorts

natural_history_and_prognosis.sex_difference: Women have better survival than men despite receiving less evidence-based treatment.

phenotype_comparisons.HFmrEF_vs_HFrEF: Overall prognosis is better in HFmrEF compared to HFrEF.
phenotype_comparisons.HFpEF_vs_HFrEF: HFpEF is generally considered to confer better survival than HFrEF, but many observational studies show the difference is negligible; a large MAGGIC meta-analysis found adjusted mortality risk for HFpEF was considerably lower than for HFrEF.

natural_history_and_prognosis.dynamics: Transition in ejection fraction over time is common; patients who progress from HFmrEF to HFrEF have worse prognosis than those who remain stable or transition to a higher EF category.
natural_history_and_prognosis.temporal_trends: Studies show survival in HF patients improved markedly between 1980 and 2000, but this positive trend may have levelled off since then.

hospitalization.temporal_trends: HF hospitalization rates peaked in the 1990s and then declined in several countries; a recent UK study (1998–2017) found age-adjusted rates of first hospitalizations increased by 28% for both all-cause and HF admissions and by 42% for non-CV admissions.
hospitalization.relative_risks: Risk of HF hospitalization is 1.5 times higher in patients with diabetes compared to controls.

content.references_and_notes: Multiple citations are present in the source text supporting the numerical estimates and statements (not included here). Abbreviations in text: HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF, CAD, BMI, HbA1c, eGFR, AF.
